title: The Missing Primitive for Agent Swarms — Lou Bichard, Ona

summary: Lou Bichard, field CTO at Owner, presents on the missing primitive for agent swarms in coding agent infrastructure. He defines a software factory as the commitment to incrementally moving humans out of the software development lifecycle, with work flowing from development to production in an automated fashion. Three patterns for running agents at scale are identified: swarms (fanning out from a single intent to multiple agents, funneling back to a PR), fleets (fanning agents across multiple repositories), and events (triggering agents via webhooks for PRs, tickets). Large companies have built internal infrastructure from scratch: Stripe's Minions drives thousands of PRs, and RAMP's Inspect manages background agents. Owner, providing development environment infrastructure for about six years, offers fleet features for automated agents across repositories. Lou introduces harness engineering as an extension of context engineering, encoding skills, agents.md, and unit tests into repositories, letting agents run, identifying where they get lost, and feeding knowledge back iteratively. The three pillars of agent swarm infrastructure are runtime (mostly solved, with Owner advocating VMs for security isolation), orchestration (solved), and coordination (unsolved). Lou demonstrates Owner's interface showing process-level sub-agents within a single VM and VM-level sub-agents spawning separate VMs with message passing. He then addresses challenges: the conceptual SDLC's five coarse steps don't match what agents need—each stage contains micro steps agents must follow deterministically. Context rot is the hardest part—agents lose track as context windows fill, skip steps, and behave sycophantically. GitHub is a poor coordination layer for agents, becoming overwhelmingly noisy for human intervention; Symphony on Linear suffers the same problem of reusing human tools for agents. Proposed solutions include state machines defining SDLC workflows, durable execution for reliable process runs, gates and compliance checking, and a CLI gateway construct that any local coding agent can invoke to verify it has completed a stage before proceeding. Lou has internal prototypes and a full spec, seeing competing approaches including graph-based workflows (NA10-type), ACPX (built on ACP), and Fabro (GitHub). He prefers releasing a standard over an implementation and notes the prototype is not built on ACP or Eight Way. He announces a virtual summit on May 6th at backgroundagents.com and a public software factory build with Zach from ONA over two weeks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Info
sections.summary: Lou Bichard introduces himself as field CTO at Owner, with previous experience as principal and platform engineer, now working with customers on the field side.

sections.title: Software Factory Definition
sections.summary: Defines software factory as the commitment to incrementally moving the human out of the loop within the SDLC, distinguishing it from individuals running parallel agents. Notes the field is extremely early.

sections.title: Agent Swarm Patterns: Swarms, Fleets, and Events
sections.summary: Introduces three patterns: swarms (fan-out from single intent funneling back to a PR), fleets (agents across multiple repos), and events (webhook-triggered agents for PRs, tickets). References backgroundagents.com.

sections.title: Real-world Agent Infrastructure Examples
sections.summary: Highlights Stripe's Minions (built on existing infrastructure, driving thousands of PRs) and RAMP's Inspect as internal agent infrastructure built from scratch.

sections.title: Owner Platform and Fleet Feature
sections.summary: Owner provides development environment infrastructure for about 6 years with fleet feature for automated agents across repos for CVE remediation, test coverage, and enforcing standards at scale.

sections.title: Harness Engineering
sections.summary: Introduces harness engineering as an extension of context engineering, encoding skills, agents.md, and unit tests into repos, letting agents run, finding where they get lost, and feeding knowledge back iteratively.

sections.title: Three Pillars: Runtime, Orchestration, and Coordination
sections.summary: Identifies runtime (solved), orchestration (solved), and coordination (unsolved) as the three infrastructure pillars. Advocates VM isolation over containers for security and avoiding noisy-neighbor problems on Kubernetes.

sections.title: Demo: Sub-agents and Fleets in Owner
sections.summary: Demonstrates Owner interface with two modes: process-level sub-agents within a single VM showing stacked agent windows, and VM-level fleet agents spawning separate VMs with message passing to a parent controlling agent. Notes UX challenges for complex sub-agent management.

sections.title: Challenges: SDLC Micro Steps and Context Rot
sections.summary: Lou asks whether a project can be built without touching code. The technology exists but challenges remain. The conceptual SDLC's five coarse steps don't map to agent reality—each stage contains micro steps that must be broken down and enforced deterministically. Context rot is the hardest part: as context windows fill, agents lose track, skip steps, and behave sycophantically to please users.

sections.title: GitHub as Poor Coordination Layer
sections.summary: GitHub is not a suitable coordination layer for agents—raising PRs, resolving merge conflicts, and fixing CI becomes incredibly noisy for humans trying to decide when to intervene. Symphony, built on Linear, suffers the same problem of reusing human tools in ways poorly suited for agents.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions: State Machines, Durable Execution, and CLI Gateways
sections.summary: Coordination may be solved through state machines defining SDLC workflows, durable execution for reliable processes, and gates and compliance checking. Lou proposes a CLI construct runnable locally or in CI that any local coding agent can invoke to verify stage completion and proceed. He has internal prototypes and a full spec available.

sections.title: Community Events and Q&A
sections.summary: Lou recaps: coordination is the missing primitive. Announces a virtual summit on May 6th at backgroundagents.com and a public software factory build with Zach from ONA over two weeks. In Q&A, he describes his CLI gateway prototype, mentions competing approaches (graph-based/NA10-type workflows, ACPX on ACP, Fabro on GitHub), and expresses preference for releasing a standard over an implementation. The prototype is not built on ACP or Eight Way protocols.
